title: Colours on a Cut-Up Decagon
statement: A convex $10$-gon with labelled vertices is divided into triangles by $7$ of its diagonals, no two of which cross in the interior of the polygon. Each vertex is to be given one of $5$ given colours so that the two endpoints of every side of the polygon and of every one of the $7$ drawn diagonals have different colours, and each of the $5$ colours is used on at least one vertex. Let $N$ be the number of such colourings, where colourings are different if some labelled vertex receives different colours. It can be shown that $N$ does not depend on which $7$ diagonals are drawn. Find the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$.
hints: There are $8$ triangles but $10$ polygon sides, so some triangle contains two sides of the polygon. Look at the vertex shared by those two sides: how many other vertices is it joined to?

Use induction on the number of vertices. A vertex shared by two polygon sides of one triangle has exactly two neighbours, and these are joined to each other, so remove it and count colourings from a palette of $k$ colours. To force all $5$ colours to appear, use inclusion-exclusion over the set of colours left out.

Start from a single triangle, which has $k(k-1)(k-2)$ colourings from a palette of $k$ colours. Each restored vertex has two neighbours of different colours, so it has $k-2$ choices. This gives $T(k)=k(k-1)(k-2)^8$ colourings of the $10$-gon for $k \ge 3$, and none for $k \le 2$. Inclusion-exclusion then gives $N=T(5)-5 \cdot T(4)+10 \cdot T(3)$, which remains to be evaluated.
solution: Call a colouring proper if the endpoints of every side and every drawn diagonal have different colours. For $k \ge 3$, we show that a triangulated convex $m$-gon has exactly $k(k-1)(k-2)^{m-2}$ proper colourings from a palette of $k$ colours, whichever triangulation is used. We use induction on $m$. For $m=3$, the three vertices are mutually joined, so there are $k(k-1)(k-2)$ proper colourings. Now let $m \ge 4$. The triangulation has $m-2$ triangles, and each of the $m$ polygon sides lies in exactly one of them. Since $m > m-2$, the pigeonhole principle gives a triangle containing at least two polygon sides, say $va$ and $vb$. This triangle fills the whole interior angle of the polygon at $v$, so no drawn diagonal leaves $v$, and the only neighbours of $v$ are $a$ and $b$. Since $m \ge 4$, the third side $ab$ of the triangle is a drawn diagonal. Removing $v$ therefore leaves a convex $(m-1)$-gon in which $ab$ is a side, and the remaining diagonals triangulate it. A proper colouring of the $m$-gon restricts to a proper colouring of the $(m-1)$-gon. Conversely, in any proper colouring of the $(m-1)$-gon, $a$ and $b$ have different colours, so $v$ can be coloured in exactly $k-2$ ways. This multiplies the count by $k-2$ and completes the induction. Hence for $m=10$ the number of proper colourings from a given palette of $k \ge 3$ colours is $$T(k)=k(k-1)(k-2)^8.$$ For $k \le 2$ there are none, because a triangle needs three colours. So $T(1)=T(2)=0$. By inclusion-exclusion over the set of colours left unused, with $\binom{5}{j}$ palettes of size $j$, $$N=T(5)-\binom{5}{4}T(4)+\binom{5}{3}T(3)-\binom{5}{2}T(2)+\binom{5}{1}T(1).$$ Here $T(5)=5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3^8=131220$, $T(4)=4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2^8=3072$ and $T(3)=3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1^8=6$. Therefore $$N=131220-5 \cdot 3072+10 \cdot 6=131220-15360+60=115920.$$ Thus $N=115920$, and the remainder when $N$ is divided by $1000$ is $920$. Why this works. mathematical-induction, inclusion-exclusion, pigeonhole: a pigeonhole count always finds a removable vertex with two adjacent neighbours, so induction fixes the palette count, and inclusion-exclusion then forces every colour to appear.

solution_figures.alt: A convex 10-gon divided into triangles by 7 non-crossing diagonals. The shaded triangle has two polygon sides, va and vb, so no diagonal leaves v and the third side ab is a drawn diagonal. Removing v leaves a triangulated 9-gon in which ab is a side.
